questions.question: Describe the costs of commuting in South African cities.
questions.expected_answer: Commuting costs money, time and effort. Public transport users pay fares, often for more than one mode, and car owners pay for fuel, maintenance, insurance, licence fees, parking, tolls and repayments. Many low-income workers spend a large share of income on transport, often more than one tenth, because apartheid planning and low-cost housing on city edges placed them far from jobs. Long trips cost hours each day, affecting family life, rest, study and health, and late workers cost businesses money.

questions.question: Explain the causes and effects of traffic congestion.
questions.expected_answer: Congestion occurs when more vehicles use a road than it can carry smoothly, mostly in the morning and afternoon peak hours. Causes include growing car numbers, cars carrying one or two people, jobs concentrated in the CBD and business nodes, unreliable trains, accidents, roadworks, broken traffic lights, vehicles stopping in lanes, poor road design and heavy trucks. Effects include lost time, wasted fuel, business losses, stress and road rage, delayed emergency vehicles and more air pollution; bus and taxi passengers also lose time.

questions.question: Describe the pollution caused by urban transport and its effects.
questions.expected_answer: Vehicle exhaust releases carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, fine particles and carbon dioxide, especially from old, poorly maintained vehicles. Smog forms when pollutants are trapped, for example by winter temperature inversions on the highveld. Effects include asthma, bronchitis and heart disease, especially for children, the elderly, the sick and people near busy roads and ranks; noise that disturbs sleep and learning; oil and rubber runoff into rivers; and greenhouse gases adding to climate change. Cost, congestion and pollution are linked in a cycle.
